claims.text: Corrosion resistance in Q235 steel is governed primarily by the integrity and composition of its native oxide layer.
The relevant native oxide layer is primarily Fe3O4-rich.
A well-developed, adherent Fe3O4-rich film protects Q235 steel against aggressive salt attack at room temperature.
A well-developed, adherent Fe3O4-rich film protects Q235 steel against aggressive salt attack at 700–900 °C.
Absence or degradation of the native oxide film accelerates corrosion of Q235 steel.
The thickness, continuity, and phase composition of the native oxide film mediate corrosion protection.
An intact Fe3O4-rich oxide film reduces ion transport to or from the Q235 substrate.
Reduced ion transport through the oxide film suppresses corrosion reactions.
Compromising or removing the oxide barrier permits easier penetration of corrosive species into the metal substrate.
Q235 specimens retaining the native oxide film will exhibit lower mass loss than polished specimens lacking the film.
Q235 specimens retaining the native oxide film will exhibit less pitting and surface degradation than polished specimens lacking the film.
The predicted benefit of retaining the oxide film will occur under both room-temperature and 700–900 °C salt exposure.
The native oxide's contribution will be less significant under mild exposure conditions.
The native oxide's contribution will be less significant when additional inhibitors or protective coatings are present.
The protective contribution of the native oxide may depend on its microstructural heterogeneity and on salt chemistry.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis refers to 'pre-exposed Q235 steel' and a protective film formed during 'initial exposure,' whereas the material initial state is described as pre-exposure Q235 already possessing an intact native oxide layer. It is therefore unclear whether the proposed film exists before the experiment or is generated by a prior exposure.
